stories.title: US / Israel – Iran
stories.detail: 9 headlines, which is about its normal of 31.5 after 30 days running. Continuing coverage rather than escalation - gold has priced this.
stories.why: The one flashpoint that hits gold through every channel at once. Safe-haven bid on the headline, Treasuries bid so nominal and real yields fall, and - uniquely - a credible threat to the Strait of Hormuz spikes crude, which lifts inflation expectations. Roughly a fifth of seaborne oil passes through that strait.
stories.counterweight: The dollar is also a haven, so risk-off bids the dollar too and cancels part of gold's gain. This is why some escalation days produce a far smaller gold move than the headlines imply.
stories.duration: Days. Gold spikes on the exchange of fire and gives most of it back within a week unless the oil disruption is real and sustained, because only then does it reach the Fed's reaction function.
stories.spoken: Iran, and the US and Israel
stories.spoken_why: It reaches gold through three channels at once: the haven bid, lower real yields, and the risk to oil coming through the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.read: Mostly not following - WTI crude, VIX, S&P 500 and 3 others are all going the other way. Either this is already in the price, or something bigger is driving the tape today.

stories.detail: 7 headlines against a normal of 22.8. Nothing that stands out from its own background.
stories.why: Two channels: haven demand, and the structural one - sanctions on Russian reserves in 2022 taught central banks that dollar reserves can be frozen, which is a large part of why official-sector gold buying has been so persistent since.
stories.counterweight: Day-to-day headlines are largely priced. The structural bid shows up in central bank demand data, not in a day's price action.
stories.duration: Headlines: days. The reserve-diversification effect: years, and it is arguably the single biggest reason gold has re-rated.
stories.spoken_why: The day to day headlines are priced, but sanctions on reserves are why central banks keep buying gold.
stories.read: Mostly not following - WTI crude, VIX, S&P 500 and 3 others are all going the other way. Either this is already in the price, or something bigger is driving the tape today.

stories.title: China / Taiwan
stories.detail: Coverage is below its own normal and carrying de-escalation language. Any risk premium here should be fading.
stories.why: Low frequency, very high severity. A genuine blockade or invasion scenario is the largest single tail risk in the gold market, because it would be a global supply-chain and reserve-currency event simultaneously.
stories.counterweight: Routine incursions and drills are so frequent they carry almost no information. Gold ignores them, correctly.
stories.duration: Drills: nothing. A real blockade: a regime change in gold pricing, not a spike.
stories.spoken_why: Routine drills mean nothing, but a genuine blockade would be the largest single risk in this market.
stories.read: Broadly consistent, though Nasdaq 100, Gold, USD/JPY and 2 others are not playing along. One asset out of line is usually its own story; several is a reason to doubt the read.

stories.title: Wider Middle East

stories.why: Haven demand, mostly. Moves gold hard on the first day of a genuine escalation and then fades, because the region's conflicts rarely touch US rate expectations directly.
stories.counterweight: Heavily discounted by markets through repetition - a headline that would have moved gold $40 in the first month of a conflict moves it $5 in the ninth.

profile.name: ADP Employment Change
profile.what: Private payroll processor's estimate of job creation, released two days before NFP at 13:15 UK.
profile.why_gold: Traded as a preview of NFP, though its correlation with the official number is poor.
profile.watch: Only really matters when it diverges wildly from the NFP forecast.
profile.gotchas: A bad predictor. Moves gold briefly, then gets forgotten by Friday.

profile.name: ISM Services PMI
profile.what: The services-sector equivalent, covering the bulk of the US economy. Released 15:00 UK.
profile.who: Institute for Supply Management, third business day of the month
profile.why_gold: More economically meaningful than the manufacturing survey and consequently a bigger mover when it surprises.
profile.watch: Prices paid, as a services-inflation signal, and employment as an NFP hint.
profile.gotchas: Noisier month to month than its manufacturing counterpart.
